bottom_line.headline: Democrats are favored to take the House
bottom_line.detail: Cook, the nonpartisan rater, expects them to gain 12 to 25 seats, and last Friday it moved two of the four Pennsylvania districts that decide the majority toward them.

bottom_line.headline: The Senate is close, tilting Democratic
bottom_line.detail: Democrats lead in Maine, Ohio, Texas and Kansas and comfortably in North Carolina; Iowa and Alaska are dead heats; and Michigan and Minnesota, two seats they must keep, both lean their way.

bottom_line.headline: Trump is deeply unpopular
bottom_line.detail: His approval is near the lowest point of his term, and presidents this far underwater usually lose seats in a midterm.

bottom_line.headline: Hochul leads comfortably in New York
bottom_line.detail: Hochul (D) is ahead of Blakeman (R) by about 13 points, and NY-17 in the Hudson Valley is still the state's only toss-up House race.

what_changed: The final polls moved Maine, Texas and Kansas toward the Democrats: Troy Jackson (D) now leads Susan Collins (R) by about 3 points, James Talarico (D) leads Ken Paxton (R) by about 3, and Adam Hamilton (D) leads Roger Marshall (R) by about 4. With North Carolina, those three are the four pickups Democrats need; each lead grew by about 1 to 2 points as final New York Times/Siena and YouGov polls entered the averages.
Ohio held: Sherrod Brown (D) leads Jon Husted (R) by about 3 points, nearly unchanged, so it remains the spare pickup if one of the other three slips.
Iowa and Alaska are still coin flips: Ashley Hinson (R) and Josh Turek (D) are tied, and Mary Peltola (D) leads Dan Sullivan (R) by about 1 point. The two newest Iowa polls both had Turek up 1.

Michigan, a seat Democrats must hold, firmed: Abdul El-Sayed (D) now leads Mike Rogers (R) by about 5 points, up from about 4, while Minnesota held with Peggy Flanagan (D) about 5 points ahead of Michele Tafoya (R).

glossary.text: A poll question that names no candidates: "Would you vote for the Democrat or the Republican for Congress in your district?" Averaged nationally, it is the best single read on which way the House is leaning. D +9 means Democrats lead by about 9 points. For scale, 2018's blue wave was about D +8 and Democrats gained 41 seats; 2022 was roughly R +3 and Republicans barely took the House.
The share of adults who approve of the president minus the share who disapprove. Negative means more people disapprove. Presidents with net approval this low usually lose seats in a midterm.

Race ratings from the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan handicapper. Toss-up means either side could win; Lean is a slight edge; Likely a clear one; Solid is not in doubt. Ratings move when polls or candidates change. Sabato's Crystal Ball (University of Virginia) is a similar nonpartisan handicapper; when it differs from Cook, the race's polls note says so.
A race whose result tends to show how the whole night is going. This year's are the four Pennsylvania seats on the House tab.

Prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi) let people bet real money on outcomes; the price is the crowd's probability. At recent prices the market thinks Democrats win the Senate about seven times in ten. It is a forecast, not a poll.
A "hold" is keeping a seat your party already has; a "pickup" (or "flip") is taking one from the other party. Democrats need four more pickups than losses to reach 51 seats.

The headline number for each Senate race is RealClearPolling's average of recent polls, which is steadier than any single survey. "Show the polls" under each race lists the latest individual polls. "Republican-leaning" or "Democratic-leaning" after a pollster means the firm works for that party or has a record of tilting that way — weigh those lighter.

Every poll is a sample. A typical one is accurate to about 3–5 points either way, so a 2-point lead is a coin flip and even a 6-point lead can flip. Averages of several polls are steadier than any one poll.
Each bar runs from the middle: blue to the left for a Democratic lead, red to the right for a Republican one. Longer means a bigger lead. A race with no bar has no recent public poll.

outlook.title: What could still change this
outlook.text: The national mood has been set since the Iran war began in February. What could still tip the close Senate races: a ceasefire or escalation, a gas-price spike, a bad week for a candidate in Texas or Maine, or the first week of early-vote turnout. A late rally or one surprising poll usually matters less than it looks.

how_to_read.title: How to read this without panicking
items: A lead of 2 points is a tie. A lead of 5 is a real edge, not a lock. Polls miss by 3–5 points in a normal year.
One poll means almost nothing. The averages on this page are what to watch, and they move slowly on purpose.
Headlines say "Democrats worry" because worry gets clicks. Check it against the numbers here before you believe it.
What would actually be bad news: the averages moving 3 or more points toward Republicans across several states at once. One state wobbling is noise.
The Senate may not be known on election night (see Election night on the My ballot tab). A slow count is not a bad count.

election_night.title: Election night
election_night.intro: Polls close in waves; counts finish on each state's own schedule. Here is what is normal, so a slow result doesn't read as a bad one.

items.what: New York (governor, NY-17, NY-26 and the local races) and most of the East count fast. North Carolina, Georgia and Ohio usually report the bulk of their vote within a few hours of polls closing.
The four Pennsylvania House seats count fast and are the first real read on the House. Trump's approval in the state is 34% (Times/Inquirer/Siena).
Texas, Iowa and Kansas typically have near-complete counts by midnight Eastern. Michigan and Minnesota can run into the early morning when close.

Maine: if nobody clears 50% of first choices (write-in candidates make that likely), the ranked-choice count happens in Augusta and took about nine days in June's primary. Alaska: by law the ranked-choice tabulation is Nov 18 and by-mail ballots count if postmarked by Nov 3, so a close race there waits two weeks.
If the Senate comes down to Maine or Alaska, control may not be known until mid-November. That is the calendar, not a sign anything went wrong.

mood.title: Why the mood is sour
mood.intro: Is it real or just headlines? Three government numbers say it's real, and none of them will move before Nov 3.

items.why: Business investment is near $4 trillion a year, and almost all of the rise since 2023 is software, chips and data centers. Investment in everything else has been flat since 2022.

items.what: Nobody's getting fired, and nobody's getting hired.
items.why: Layoffs are near record lows, but hiring has slid back to 2016 levels and fewer people quit than before the pandemic. People have jobs; they don't have options.

items.what: Prices are rising faster than paychecks again.
items.why: Wages are up 3.0% over the past year; prices are up 3.7%. The lines crossed this year for the first time since 2023, so the average worker is losing ground.
items.source: Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI and average hourly earnings

early_vote.party_intro: In states that register voters by party, registered Democrats are a bigger share of the early vote than at the same point in 2024; estimates for Georgia and Texas point the same way. Nationally, about 11 million registered Democrats and 8 million registered Republicans had voted early by Sunday.
early_vote.party_source: Decision Desk HQ, Nov 1. Georgia and Texas don't register voters by party; those shares are estimates.
means: In the Senate states with party data, the early vote leans more Democratic than it did at the same point in 2024. Democrats have leaned toward early voting since 2020, but these comparisons are early vote against early vote, so that habit is already counted: in most of these states, Republicans are a smaller share of the early vote than two years ago.
Some of the jump in early voting may be people switching from Election Day, so it doesn't show how many will vote in all.

It is not a forecast. A party registration is not a vote, unaffiliated voters (about a third of North Carolina's early vote) could go either way, and Election Day voters have leaned Republican in recent elections, so the count can shift toward Republicans as Election Day votes are counted.

New York and its counties don't publish the party makeup of early voters, so there is no read on how Western New York's early voters lean. About 65% of the state's early votes came from outside New York City, and Erie County's Republican chairman said, in WBFO's report, that the number of Republican early voters is up from past years, without giving figures.
Decision Desk HQ's read: the early vote is "spooky for GOP — but not fatal." It fits a Democratic-leaning year in the polls; it doesn't say who wins Maine, Ohio or Texas.
